demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one. Snake-related and pregnancy/birth reminders imply trauma contexts unrelated to bereavement, and there is no supporting threat or memory content linking them to this loss.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons similarly implies a trauma context involving violence, combat, or armed threat, which is unsupported by the stated trauma type and by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to justify unless the death specifically involved childbirth or infant loss; nothing else in the profile supports that context. This makes the trigger clinically implausible relative to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons implies a trauma context involving combat, assault, or armed responders. That does not fit the rest of this bereavement-focused profile and is not supported by the other trigger, threat, or strategy items, so it appears incoherent with the trauma type and overall formulation.

vignette: Sanjay's life had been defined by color palettes and client deadlines until the night his mother's phone rang in the cramped hallway of their San Francisco apartment. He had just finished a sketch of a minimalist living room when the call came. The voice on the other end was thin, the tone urgent. "Sanjay, she-" the line crackled, and the next word he heard was "died." The word hung like a weight, the world tilting until the ceiling seemed to close in. In that instant, his body surged: his heart hammered, his palms sweated, and his mind spiraled into a vivid, unbidden replay of his mother's breathless whispering and the ambulance lights that burst into his living room that morning. The experience was more than a shock; it became a flashback that would echo through his days. Months after that night, Sanjay found himself avoiding the very dates that once felt ordinary. The anniversary of his mother's death, the date he had planned a celebratory dinner with his wife Maya, became a minefield of dread. When the calendar lit up with the exact day, he would close his laptop and force himself to leave the office before the clock struck five. Even when Maya suggested a simple walk in the park on that day, he'd steer the conversation toward neutral topics, hoping to sidestep any mention of loss. He began rehearsing worst-case scenarios in the quiet of his studio, picturing himself unable to sleep, his body reacting to imagined danger before he could even think it. The rehearsals were intended to "prepare" him, but they instead amplified the flashbacks, making his chest tighten each time a memory flashed, and his anger flared over trivial office mishaps. In the same months, the simple trigger of a colleague's comment about a recent funeral became a spark for a full-blown threat. When the coworker laughed, "Just another funeral, right?" Sanjay's mind instantly flooded with the image of his mother's coffin and the heartrending silence that followed. The body's reflexive reaction-a racing heartbeat, a sudden cold sweat-preceded any rational thought. He would leave the meeting room in a hurry, eyes darting to the door, feeling an urgent need to escape what felt like an imminent danger. The flashbacks would recur whenever he heard words of loss, and the physical threat response intensified his sense of impending catastrophe. These loops tightened when Sanjay began to avoid any reminders of grief. He stopped listening to the memorial playlist that used to accompany his late mother's favorite songs, removed the framed photograph from the wall, and even asked Maya to avoid mentioning her own late father. He could not bear the sight of a cemetery's quiet path, so he cancelled a weekend trip that included a drive past the city's memorial park. His interior design studio, once a sanctuary of creativity, felt increasingly claustrophobic; the very walls seemed to press against him when he tried to focus on a client's vision. The avoidance of anniversaries, funeral topics, and grief reminders only amplified the flashback intensity whenever a memory slipped through. The threat responses-flashes, bodily pre-mind reactions, irritability-forced him to rehearse worst-case scenarios even more obsessively, and each rehearsal brought new, sharper images of his mother's final moments, further entrenching the cycle. The threat of a flashback during a client presentation grew so severe that he began to miss deadlines. He would arrive late, his hands shaking as he organized his sketches, and when a client's eyes focused on his design, he could not maintain the calm. Anger erupted at the smallest misstep; a misplaced measurement or a wrong choice of trim would trigger an explosive outburst, leaving Maya feeling alienated by the sudden harshness. The irritation became a shield, a way to distance himself from the raw pain that flooded whenever his body reacted before his mind could process. Yet the irritability only magnified the threat, convincing him that the world was unsafe and that he had to remain perpetually on guard. The cycle-triggers leading to threat, threat leading to maladaptive rehearsal and avoidance, avoidance reinforcing threat-crept further into his professional and personal life. By early spring, Sanjay's work suffered noticeably; clients began to notice a change in tone, and Maya's patience thinned. He started arriving late to dinner, muttering about his "bad luck" with design details that were, in fact, symptoms of an underlying terror. When Maya finally asked what was wrong, he could not articulate the knot inside him, only the sense that he was constantly on the brink of another flashback. It was during a tense conversation about a new client's color scheme that Sanjay realized he could no longer function in the present. The relentless rehearsal of worst-case outcomes had become a fog that clouded his judgment, and the avoidance of any trigger had left him isolated. Sanjay's decision to seek therapy was precipitated by a night when he dreamed of his mother's bedroom again, the lights dimmed, and a cold wind slipped through the window. He woke in a sweat, heart hammering, unable to return to his apartment's quiet because the memories flooded back with terrifying clarity. He now fears that each flashback will unravel his marriage and career, but he also hopes that confronting these memories might bring him the peace that has been missing since that fateful night.
